claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy can maintain structural and chemical stability by suppressing short-range order and grain-boundary elemental segregation.
The initiation of short-range order and elemental segregation causes secondary-phase formation.
A one-hour dwell at each annealing temperature allows atomic diffusion while avoiding extraneous contamination.
Short-range ordering and grain-boundary segregation drive broader elemental segregation and act as precursors to secondary phases.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy maintains a uniformly distorted lattice with minimal short-range order.
Minimal short-range order preserves the single-phase solid solution.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility and can induce local ordering, segregation, nanoscale precipitation, or phase separation.
Precipitation or phase separation disrupts the uniform structural matrix.
Thermally induced microstructural changes alter catalytic activity.
Thermally induced microstructural changes alter thermoelectric properties.
Nanoparticles that remain homogeneous single-phase solid solutions retain catalytic performance similar to the initial baseline.
Nanoparticles that remain homogeneous single-phase solid solutions retain thermoelectric performance similar to the initial baseline.
Samples exhibiting short-range order or minor phase separation will concurrently show measurable changes in catalytic turnover rate.
Samples exhibiting short-range order or minor phase separation will concurrently show measurable changes in Seebeck coefficient or electrical conductivity.
XRD, TEM, and EDS can identify the proposed onset of short-range order, segregation, or secondary-phase formation.
The temperature at which short-range order and segregation become significant depends on compositional variation and processing history.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify avoiding rapid quenching, whereas the falsification experiment explicitly requires rapid quenching after annealing.
